Physical reasoning: The stripper temperature is governed by the enthalpy balance of the stripping column, where live steam (measured directly as xmeas_19, and set via the steam valve xmv_9) is the dominant energy inflow that raises the liquid/vapor temperature on the trays (an accumulation-of-energy analog of a mass balance, since ΔT ~ net heat rate / heat capacity). I include both the measured steam flow (xmeas_19, most direct physical driver, expected +) and the valve command (xmv_9, expected + as it acts on the same physical channel with some dynamic lag/nonlinearity relative to the measured flow) as two proxies for the same energy-inflow term, since actuator saturation/dead-time may make them not perfectly collinear. I also include the stripper's own pressure (xmeas_16, same unit — permitted since it's not a neighboring-unit variable) as a same-vessel accumulation-state term: higher pressure in the stripper is associated with more retained vapor/energy holdup and correlates with higher equilibrium temperature, so its expected sign is also positive. The bias term c[4] captures any small constant drift and is not given a theoretical sign.

I deliberately excluded xmeas_31/xmeas_25/xmeas_29/xmeas_38 (composition/analyzer variables) from this generation since those would represent a Dalton's-law/VLE mechanism (a different law category) and mixing them in here would violate the single-law commitment; if this mass/energy-balance law's sign check fails, the next attempt will pivot to the VLE law using a composition term properly scaled by a pressure reference instead.

Both previous energy/mass-balance attempts failed the sign check on xmeas_19 and xmeas_16, which strongly suggests those "direct physical" flow/pressure proxies are actually contaminated by the base-layer PI-control loop: the steam flow measurement xmeas_19 already reflects the controller's compensatory reaction to the *previous* temperature deviation, not a pure open-loop energy inflow, so its lagged correlation with Δy comes out with the "wrong" (negative) sign — a classic closed-loop confound, not a physics-defying result. Rather than re-labeling the mechanism to justify that sign, I am switching law categories entirely, as instructed.

I now commit to the Control-law category (#6): xmv_9 (Stripper Steam Valve) is the manipulated variable that the base-layer stripper-temperature PI controller directly drives to track a temperature setpoint, and it is the single MIC-selected variable most proximate to actuation (no intermediate flow-measurement or same-unit accumulation-state term that could reintroduce feedback confounding). Because the valve command precedes the flow response and the flow response precedes the thermal response, using the valve position alone (rather than the already-controller-adjusted flow measurement) should better isolate the feed-forward, physically-causal direction: opening the steam valve increases live-steam energy input to the column trays, raising Δy(t). I therefore expect a clean positive coefficient on xmv_9.

I deliberately dropped xmeas_19 and xmeas_16 this round to isolate whether the manipulated-variable-only model passes the sign check; if xmv_9 also fails, that would indicate the confounding is even deeper (e.g., xmv_9 itself lags the temperature error by less than one sample so it also inherits the reactive sign), and the next step would be to pivot to a genuine mass-balance target using flow variables that are NOT part of this control loop (e.g. reactor feed rate xmeas_6 or purge rate xmeas_10) as exogenous drivers instead of assuming stripper-internal actuators are open-loop.

Gen 2's simple control-law model (xmv_9 alone) passed its sign check, confirming that the steam-valve command is a valid feed-forward proxy for the energy inflow to the stripper column, uncontaminated by the closed-loop confound that killed the xmeas_19/xmeas_16 attempts. Rather than abandoning that validated direction, I am refining it toward the underlying valve/orifice physics: real control valves rarely have a purely linear flow-vs-position characteristic (equal-percentage and quick-opening trims are common), so the actual live-steam mass flow — and hence the heat delivered to the trays — is better approximated as a low-order polynomial in valve position rather than a pure linear term. I add xmv_9^2 as the leading nonlinear correction term of the flow characteristic Q = Cv*f(x)*sqrt(ΔP), holding ΔP roughly constant across the short 1-step horizon so that f(x) ≈ a*x + b*x^2 locally.

I avoided sqrt(xmv_9) after Gen 3's DomainError revealed that the raw xmv_9 series in this dataset can take small negative values (likely due to noise/normalization around a near-zero-opening valve state), which breaks any fractional/sqrt exponent applied directly to the raw variable. Using only integer powers (xmv_9, xmv_9^2) sidesteps that domain issue entirely while still capturing valve nonlinearity.

Both c[1] and c[2] are expected positive since higher valve opening (in either the linear or quadratic regime) should only increase steam flow and thus increase stripper temperature, never decrease it — a violation of this sign (especially for c[1], which already passed once) would be strong evidence of confounding requiring a pivot away from this actuator-based approach entirely (e.g., toward reactor-feed-rate mass balance using xmeas_6).

Using the stripper's own pressure (xmeas_16, same unit, permitted) as a local proxy for the driving pressure head, I construct the multiplicative interaction term xmv_9*sqrt(|xmeas_16|), which represents the actual nonlinear steam mass flow rather than a linear valve-position proxy alone. I retain the linear xmv_9 term as a first-order fallback in case the valve is frequently near-saturated (where sqrt(ΔP) contribution is nearly constant and the response looks locally linear in x), and c[3] remains an unconstrained drift term. I used abs() inside sqrt to avoid the DomainError encountered in Gen 3, since transient negative or noisy pressure readings should not crash evaluation, though physically xmeas_16 (stripper pressure) should be strictly positive in normal operation.

For this generation, I am testing whether the bias/drift term c[2] in Gen 2 was actually helping or just adding unnecessary complexity: since the model represents a physical rate-of-change relationship (Δy over a fixed short sampling interval) driven purely by valve opening, there is no strong theoretical reason for a nonzero constant drift term absent any other driver — a persistent bias would imply the process drifts even at zero average valve command, which is not physically expected in steady operation. Removing c[2] tests a strictly simpler, purely proportional control-law form (Δy = c[1]*xmv_9), which, if it retains a similar RMSE to Gen 2 while reducing parameter count, should yield a better fitness score without reintroducing any of the confounded accumulation-state variables. If this single-term model's RMSE degrades substantially compared to Gen 2, that would indicate the bias term was capturing a real (if small) systematic offset, and the next step would be to reintroduce a minimal bias term while keeping the valve term as the sole physical driver.

Gen 2, 4, and 8 all confirmed that xmv_9 (steam valve command) alone is the single validated, sign-consistent, feed-forward driver of stripper temperature change, uncontaminated by the closed-loop confound that poisoned every attempt using measured steam flow (xmeas_19) or stripper pressure (xmeas_16), whether added linearly (Gen 1) or multiplicatively as a pressure-head term (Gen 6) — both of those repeatedly failed sign check, confirming they reflect the PI controller's reactive compensation to the *previous* temperature error rather than genuine open-loop drivers. Gen 7's naive cubic polynomial in xmv_9 also failed sign check, most likely because an unconstrained odd-power term can flip sign in response to noise near zero and doesn't respect the physical constraint that valve opening (regardless of direction) can only ever increase, never decrease, the magnitude of steam admission.

To capture genuine valve/orifice nonlinearity (Law 4) while staying strictly within the validated actuator-only channel, I replace the failed cubic term with a signed square-root term, xmv_9*sqrt(abs(xmv_9)), which behaves like |xmv_9|^1.5 with the sign of xmv_9 preserved. This is a common intermediate nonlinearity between a linear valve trim and a full quadratic amplification, and unlike a bare sqrt(xmv_9) (which crashed in Gen 3 due to small negative values in the normalized signal) or a bare cubic (wrong-signed in Gen 7), this construction is guaranteed to have the same sign as xmv_9 itself at every point, so it cannot introduce a sign flip through noise — its coefficient should theoretically be positive for the same reason as the linear term: more valve opening (in the same direction) can only increase heat/steam delivery to the trays, never decrease it.

If this signed-square-root term's fitted coefficient fails the sign check, that would be strong evidence that all higher-order nonlinear corrections to the xmv_9 signal are just fitting actuator noise rather than a real valve trim curve, and the next step would be to abandon nonlinear corrections entirely and accept the simplest linear-only Gen 8 model as the ceiling for this actuator-only, confound-free approach — potentially pivoting toward a genuinely different unit's flow variable (e.g., xmeas_6 reactor feed rate or xmeas_10 purge rate) under a true mass-balance law instead.

Gen 4 additionally showed that adding a quadratic xmv_9^2 term (representing the nonlinear valve-trim characteristic, still purely a function of the same validated actuator signal) PASSED its sign check with both c[1] and c[2] positive, confirming that within-actuator nonlinearity is a legitimate refinement of this control-law channel, not a new confounded pathway.

However, Gen 4's version included an extra unconstrained bias term c[3], and Gen 8 subsequently showed that removing the (unjustified, physically unmotivated) bias term from the pure-linear model improved the fitness score even though RMSE ticked up slightly — indicating the evaluation's parsimony penalty rewards dropping the physically-unnecessary constant-drift term. This tests whether the quadratic term's RMSE improvement (0.0952 in Gen 4 vs 0.0962 in Gen 8) survives removing the bias term, which should reduce parameter count and potentially yield a better fitness than both Gen 4 (bias-laden quadratic) and Gen 8 (bias-free linear only).

If this bias-free quadratic model's sign check still passes (as expected, since both terms are monotonic non-negative-in-magnitude functions of the same validated actuator channel), and its fitness beats Gen 8, that would establish that the quadratic valve-trim nonlinearity is a genuine, worthwhile refinement once stripped of unnecessary bias. This generation tries a different, still strictly actuator-only nonlinearity that is physically motivated by real control-valve trim characteristics: many steam control valves (especially for utility/heating duty) have an "equal-percentage" trim, where flow response to stem position is exponential rather than polynomial: Q ≈ Cv·(R^x - 1) for rangeability R, which is equivalent to Cv·(exp(k·x) - 1) for a positive gain constant k = ln(R). This is a genuine instance of the valve/orifice flow-characteristic law (Law 4), just with an exponential (rather than polynomial) nonlinearity in valve position — a form that many real steam trims actually follow much more closely than a power-series expansion. Both c[1] (overall scale linking increased steam admission to stripper-tray temperature rise) and c[2] (the trim's equal-percentage gain constant) are expected positive, since greater valve opening should only ever increase steam delivery and thus Δy, never decrease it, and a positive c[2] captures the characteristic's increasing/convex shape.

Unlike the earlier sqrt/cubic attempts, this exponential form is smooth, monotonic, and has no domain restrictions (unlike sqrt, which crashed on negative xmv_9 values in Gen 3), and it does not introduce any new potentially-confounded physical variable — it stays entirely within the validated xmv_9-only channel. If this fails its sign check, that would be strong evidence that ALL nonlinear corrections to the raw xmv_9 signal are essentially fitting actuator/noise artifacts rather than a genuine valve-trim curve, and the next step would be to accept Gen 8's pure linear model as the ceiling for this channel and pivot toward a genuinely different, non-stripper-actuator variable (e.g., xmeas_6 reactor feed rate as an upstream mass-balance driver, Law 1) instead of continuing to refine xmv_9's functional form.

This generation proposes a genuine valve/orifice saturation nonlinearity that is guaranteed, by construction, to never flip sign relative to xmv_9: a rational (Langmuir-type) saturation form Δy = c1*xmv_9/(1+c2*xmv_9^2). For small xmv_9 this reduces to the already-validated linear term c1*xmv_9 (matching Gen 8's passing model), while for larger |xmv_9| the denominator's positive quadratic term progressively suppresses the response — physically representing real control-valve/critical-flow saturation (steam mass flow through an orifice approaches a choked-flow ceiling as valve opening or pressure drop characteristics saturate, so the flow-vs-position curve is concave rather than unbounded-linear or -quadratic). Both numerator gain c1 and denominator saturation coefficient c2 are expected positive: c1 because more valve opening in the unsaturated region can only increase heat delivery, and c2 because a positive denominator coefficient only ever attenuates (never reverses) the numerator's sign, consistent with a physical flow ceiling rather than a reversal of flow direction. Unlike the exponential and cubic forms, this construction cannot introduce a spurious sign flip through fitting noise, since c1*xmv_9/(1+c2*xmv_9^2) has the same sign as xmv_9 for any real c2 ≥ 0. If this fails its sign check, that would indicate all valve-nonlinearity refinements are exhausted for this confound-free channel, and future generations should pivot entirely to a different, non-stripper-actuator, non-accumulation-state variable such as xmeas_6 (reactor feed rate) as an upstream mass-balance driver under Law 1.
